newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - Jan 22.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - Jan 22.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
DAILY TELEGRAPH
-- BRITANNIA ACTS TO CURB WINDFALL SPECULATORS

Britannia Building Society, which next month makes the first payments under its mutuality package, yesterday suspended the opening of instant access accounts after new accounts increased twelve times, mainly through savers hoping to benefit if the society converts. Britannia said the swell in numbers was affecting service and that it had no plans to convert.
-- MILLWALL HEADS INTO ADMINISTRATION
Millwall Holdings will today put itself into administration in an attempt to rescue the Millwall Football Club, which yesterday was forced by creditors to suspend share dealings.

Administration means the company remains a going concern, allowing fixtures to continue. Advisers were seeking agreement with bankers NatWest to allow fresh capital to be raised through a rights issue.
-- LIFE SCIENCES TAKEOVER NETS BBC BOSS 3 MILLION POUNDS

BBC chairman Sir Christopher Bland will receive 3.1 million pounds stg after agreeing to an American takeover of scientific instruments manufacturing company Life Sciences International, which he also chairs. Thermo Instrument Systems yesterday announced a 236 million pound cash bid for the company, which has steadily lost value over the past five years.
THE TIMES
-- CBI BACKS CLARKE OVER BASE RATES -- FOR NOW

The latest quarterly industrial trends survey by the Confederation of British Industry suggests that the Chancellor, Kenneth Clark, is right to leave base rates on hold. A spokesman for the CBI said that sterling's strength was beginning to feed through to manufacturers' export orders and that no interest rate increase is justified at the present time. A Treasury spokesman said it was clear sterling's recent strength had helped to keep industry cost pressures very subdued.
-- NISSAN UK WINS BATTLE FOR JOBS

Nissan UK have secured the creation of thousands of jobs in Britain, with UK managers winning the battle with bosses in Japan. An extra 800 workers will be employed at the Sunderland plant to build a new mid-sized family car, with a further 2,700 jobs created at Nissan's supplier base in the area. Nissan headquarters had initially wanted to build the car in Japan, but tough negotiations convinced them that Nissan's global aims were best served by production in Britain.
-- PENSION CHIEFS FACE PIA GRILLING

The Personal Investment Authority (PIA) are summoning insurance companies suspected of slow reactions to the pensions mis-selling review to a series of secret meetings. Colette Bowe, the chief executive of the PIA, has decided to get tough with the worst offenders and has warned them they must resolve most of their cases by the end of this year. Ms Bowe is believed to have told firms already seen that if necessary they must double the number of staff assigned to the review.
THE GUARDIAN
-- FED CHIEF TALKS UP ECONOMY

US Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan yesterday gave a positive verdict on the state of the US economy, easing fears of an imminent interest rates rise. He said that growth was strong and inflationary pressure minor, but hinted that policy may need tightening in the medium term.
-- TUBE SELL-OFF THREAT FADES

The prospect of the London Tube network being privatised appeared to diminish yesterday, as it emerged that some ministers view the proposal as a vote-loser. The first stage of a "Save our Tube" campaign is to be launched today by the Lord Mayor of London, which will urge government to commit to long-term, consistent funding of the network.
-- HORLICK "DEAL" DEALT A BLOW

Nicola Horlick's campaign to be reinstated at Morgan Grenfell suffered yesterday when a senior Frankfurt official backed the London office. Rolf Breuer, due to take over as Deutsche Bank chief executive in May, said that it was clear Mrs Horlick intended to damage the bank by attempting to poach staff for a defection to ABN Amro. Mrs Horlick denies this.
THE INDEPENDENT
-- ROYAL BANK SPEARHEADS INTERNET REVOLUTION

The Royal Bank of Scotland will launch the first full-fledged Internet service in the spring. The move puts RBS at the spearhead of a revolution in banking and ahead of its high street rivals who are mostly only at the experimental stage with direct linked home banking service. RBS will offer Internet banking to 500,000 telephone customers initially who will be able to conduct a variety of banking services through the Internet, providing they have the necessary equipment: a personal computer with Microsoft Windows and access to the Internet.
-- BOEING CALLS HALT ON $7 BILLION SUPER-JUMBO PROJECT

Boeing announced yesterday that it is shelving plans to build a stretched version of its 747 jumbo jet, saying that the market was too small to justify the cost of the programme, estimated to be around $US7 billion. The move by Boeing leaves Airbus Industrie as the only jet manufacturer preparing to launch a super-jumbo.
-- GOVERNMENT BLOCKS FRENCH BID FOR MID KENT WATER

President of the board of trade, Ian Lang, yesterday blocked a hostile takeover of Mid Kent Holdings, made jointly by two French companies, General Utilities and Saur. The ban on the takeover follows an investigation by the Monopolies and Mergers Commission, which found that the deal would be against the public interest as General Utilities and Saur respectively own the neighboring Folkestone and Dover Water Services and South East Water. The decision ends months of uncertainty for Mid Kent.
